clue.text: US city, place with a novel location

parts.note: LA is the usual short form of Los Angeles
to place something is to put it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A travel note pairing an American city with a spot that turns up in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Laputa is the flying island Gulliver visits in Swift's novel, so 'novel location' is a place in a book rather than a fresh site.
explanation.definitionFit: Laputa is the floating island in Gulliver's Travels, a setting invented for a work of fiction.

clue.text: Exam is not entirely fair everyone gets put out

indicators.note: the word for everyone is pushed apart, put out of shape, to take another piece inside it

parts.note: everyone means all

indicators.note: not entirely means the last letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: fair, as in an even contest, means even

explanation.surface: A complaint that an examination is unfair and has upset all the candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' drops the last letter of the synonym for fair; 'gets put out' means everyone is disturbed, opened up to take that piece. 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An A level is the British school-leaving examination taken at around eighteen.

clue.text: Not having enough employees to work in secret

definitions.text: Not having enough employees to work
definitions.meaning: short of hands, that is of workers, for the job
done slyly and deceitfully, out of sight

explanation.surface: A firm too short-staffed to operate is also running a covert operation.
explanation.definitionFit: Short of hands means understaffed, and the same word describes sly, deceitful behaviour done in secret.

clue.text: See us after a fight, carrying silver spears?

indicators.note: the fight carries silver along with it, so silver follows straight on
us comes after the other pieces, so it goes at the end

parts.note: taken as written
to spar is to fight, as boxers do in practice
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone arranges to meet after a brawl, bringing silver lances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a link word inviting us along; the question mark marks spears as a definition by example, since asparagus shoots are called spears.
explanation.definitionFit: Asparagus is sold as spears, its edible young shoots, so the vegetable is defined by that cooks' term.

clue.text: Drunk's to be absent from church service, causing confusion

indicators.note: a drunk slurs his esses, so the words are said as a tipsy speaker would say them

parts.words: to be absent from church service
parts.note: to be absent from is to miss, and the Catholic church service is Mass

explanation.surface: A drunkard skipping Mass throws everything into disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: MISS MASS, said with a drunken slur turning each final S sound into SH, comes out as the answer. 'causing' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A jumbled, disordered mixture is a hotchpotch, a state of confusion.

clue.text: Big tent with brand new inner part

parts.note: a marque is a brand, especially of car

indicators.note: the inner part of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A large tent fitted with a brand-new inner section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inner part' of 'new' is its middle letter E; 'new' is not N here.
explanation.definitionFit: A marquee is a large tent used for parties and shows.

clue.text: Endless criticism written about old philosopher

indicators.note: the trimmed word is written around another letter
endless means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: stick is informal for criticism, as in giving someone stick

explanation.surface: A complaint that ancient thinkers are endlessly criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts STICK to STIC; 'written about' wraps that round O. STICK as 'criticism' is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stoic was a follower of Zeno's school of ancient Greek philosophy.

clue.text: Crackers manufactured to be pulled finally

indicators.note: the final letter is pulled away

parts.note: something manufactured is made

explanation.surface: Christmas crackers are made in order to be pulled in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about Christmas crackers, novelty tubes pulled apart at British festive meals; 'Crackers' is really slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackers is British slang for crazy, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Foreign ruler entertains king aboard ship on such a sea?

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed after the other pieces
aboard means inside the ship, so the piece goes between its letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in as a guest, so the ruler holds the king inside

parts.note: an aga is a Turkish or Ottoman commander or chief
R is short for rex, Latin for king
such means so, as in so much

explanation.surface: A foreign potentate hosts a king on board a vessel on some sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertains' and 'aboard' are both containers, nested; 'on' places the last piece after them in this down clue. The question mark flags that the Sargasso is a sea with no coasts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic named for its floating seaweed.

clue.text: Fellow pedlars circulating mineral

indicators.note: circulating means moving around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fellow travelling salesmen go round hawking a mineral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' looks like an adjective for the pedlars, but it is just F; 'circulating' tells you to rearrange the pedlars.
explanation.definitionFit: Feldspar is a common rock-forming mineral, an aluminium silicate.

clue.text: Directs leader away from Scottish region

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off

parts.note: the Borders is the region of Scotland next to England

explanation.surface: Someone instructs a leader to leave part of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is the Scottish region along the English border; 'leader away from' removes its first letter B.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct people is to give them orders, so both are verbs of command.

clue.text: Alarm triggered initially by mistake

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word triggered

parts.note: a mistake is an error

explanation.surface: An alarm went off because someone made a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes T from 'triggered'; 'by' links it to ERROR.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror and alarm are both states of great fear, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: Cryptic clue's written about North America —- with this as definition?

definitions.text: Cryptic clue's written about North America —- with this as definition?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are written around the next piece
cryptic means puzzling or jumbled, so the letters of the following word are mixed

explanation.surface: A wry aside that a crossword clue about North America needs this as its definition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' rearranges the clue's letters; 'written about' wraps them round N. The whole clue then hints that the answer is how one would personify America.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the cartoon figure personifying the United States government and nation.

clue.text: Run reports on cricketers

parts.note: in cricket an extra is a run not scored off the bat
a reporter covers a story

explanation.surface: A news item about a cricket team, with a run of reports.
explanation.walkthrough: Extra cover is a fielding position in cricket, so the plural names fielders standing there; 'Run' is a cricket extra, not a jog.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra covers are fielders placed at the extra-cover position on the off side in cricket.

clue.text: Upset to hear guests dispute what's been decided

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A host is dismayed to hear that guests are quarrelling over a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges the letters of TO HEAR GUESTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To argue the toss is a British idiom for disputing a decision already made.

clue.text: Type of car — journalist's shown round faulty batch

indicators.note: the journalist goes round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: a hack is a journalist; the possessive is no letter

indicators.note: faulty means broken, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A reporter is shown around a defective batch of cars of one model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faulty' rearranges the batch letters into TCHBA, and 'shown round' wraps the journalist round them. Hack is mildly disparaging slang for a journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchback is a car with a rear door that lifts up, a body style.

clue.text: Extremely short cheese tasting event?

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese
a fest is a festival or gathering, here one for tasting

explanation.surface: A very brief festival for sampling cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' is not a deletion signal; it makes 'short' a superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of brief means shortest, short in the extreme degree.

clue.text: Deals with worker trapped by CIA plant

parts.note: deals are trades

indicators.note: trapped by means held inside the following letters

parts.note: a worker ant is the classic crossword worker

explanation.surface: An agent doing deals is caught in a CIA sting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a spy planted by the CIA; it is the definition, a botanical plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Tradescantia is a genus of flowering plants, the spiderworts, often grown as houseplants.

clue.text: Case of a horse being nobbled by racing expert

parts.note: taken as written
TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle races on the Isle of Man

indicators.note: nobbled means seized, so the horse is caught inside the other letters

parts.note: an ace is an expert
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A racing tipster is caught nobbling a horse, a case for the stewards.
explanation.walkthrough: To nobble a racehorse is to drug or tamper with it, so 'being nobbled by' puts the horse inside the racing expert. Horse as heroin is drug slang.
explanation.definitionFit: An attaché case is a small hard briefcase, so the short form names that case.

clue.text: Became cornered by snake in Andean city

indicators.note: cornered means boxed in, so this piece is held inside the snake

parts.note: a boa is a constricting snake
to got is to become, as in got angry

explanation.surface: Someone was trapped by a snake in a South American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cornered by' signals containment: the snake encloses the verb. Got as 'became' is the sense in 'got angry'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bogotá, capital of Colombia, stands high in the Andes mountains.

clue.text: Whacked an idle so-and-so

definitions.meaning: whacked is British slang for exhausted, worn out

explanation.surface: Someone thumped a lazy layabout.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead beat means utterly exhausted, and as one word it is a lazy, feckless person.

clue.text: Inaccessible place, one located in built-up East Sussex town

indicators.note: located in means placed inside the next letters
in a down clue, built-up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Rye is a town in East Sussex
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A remote spot found in a developed town in East Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East Sussex' is one county name in the surface, but East gives E and Sussex town gives RYE (a small town in that county). I goes between them (EIRYE), and 'built-up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is an eagle's nest built high on a crag, so figuratively a remote, hard-to-reach place.

clue.text: Gangster loves to bring bad luck

parts.note: a hood is a gangster, short for hoodlum
love means zero in tennis, and each looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A mobster loves to bring others misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb, hoodoo means to jinx, so it fits 'bring bad luck'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoodoo someone is to put a jinx on them, bringing them misfortune.

clue.text: Busy person needs a pager, perhaps

parts.note: a busy bee is a hard-working person
a means per, as in so much a head or per head

explanation.surface: A busy professional needs a pager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is not taken as written: it means PER, as in ten pounds a day.
explanation.definitionFit: A pager is one example of a device that beeps to alert its owner.

clue.text: Brit abroad is to clean up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to mop is to clean a floor

explanation.surface: A British expatriate has to tidy up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses MOP. Pom is Australian slang for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Pom is Australian and New Zealand slang for a British person.

clue.text: Escort and companion assigned to a former dictator

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour
taken as written
Juan Perón was the military ruler of Argentina

explanation.surface: A bodyguard and aide are assigned to a deposed strongman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'companion' is the British honour CH, not CHAP; 'assigned to' just joins it to A PERON.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon accompanies and supervises, especially a young woman, acting as an escort.

clue.text: Beastly charge impressed European

parts.note: impressed, as in pressed with a mark, means stamped

explanation.surface: A European was struck by a brutal accusation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' suggests nastiness; here it means made by beasts, a charge of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden mass rush of panicking cattle or other animals, a charge.

clue.text: Alcohol mostly rejected with expression of contempt in North African quarter

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word reads backwards
mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: sake is Japanese rice wine
bah is an exclamation of contempt

explanation.surface: Drink is mostly refused with a scornful snort in a Moroccan quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims the drink to SAK; 'rejected' turns that back to KAS. A kasbah is a walled old quarter, as in Algiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A kasbah is the old citadel quarter of a North African city.
